panels.description: Turns completed per second, across every outcome (success, error, timeout, cancelled, client_error). This is the top-line traffic indicator for the turn path — watch it for unexpected drops (traffic stopped reaching this service) or spikes (a retry storm, or a new heavy caller).
panels.title: Turn rate

panels.description: The share of turns that ended in outcome=error or outcome=timeout, out of all turns. client_error (the caller sent bad input) is deliberately excluded, since that isn't a service failure. Healthy is close to 0%; a sustained rise means turns are genuinely failing — check 'Turn rate by outcome' below to see which outcome is driving it, then the LLM/Tools/Dependencies rows to find where in the turn it originates.
panels.title: Turn error %

panels.description: The slowest 1% of successful turns, in seconds. This is the number users actually feel — if it climbs, conversations are getting slower even with no errors. Compare against 'Turn duration: p50/p95/p99' to see if it's a gradual drift or a sudden step, and against the LLM/Tools p95 panels to see which downstream call is contributing the latency.
panels.title: p99 turn duration

panels.description: The share of calls to the LLM (any backend — direct, gateway, or sidecar) that returned an error, out of all LLM calls. A spike usually means an upstream LLM provider or the LLM gateway is degraded — check 'LLM failure % by reason' for the specific reason, and 'LLM request rate by backend' to see if one backend in particular is affected.
panels.title: LLM failure %

panels.description: The share of agent tool calls that failed, out of all tool calls, across every tool kind (builtin, extension, MCP, etc). A rise means agents are failing to use their tools — check 'Tool error % by kind' to isolate which kind is failing, and 'Tool error categories' for the specific failure reason.
panels.title: Tool error %

panels.description: How many service-agents API pods are currently responding to a metrics scrape (excludes the separate builtin-resources deployment). This is a basic 'is the service actually running' check — 0 means Prometheus can't see any pod at all, which is worse than any error rate above, since none of the other numbers on this dashboard can be trusted while this is 0.
panels.title: Pods up

panels.description: How many ExecuteTurn calls are being processed right now, across all pods. A sustained climb without a matching rise in 'Turn rate' can mean turns are piling up rather than completing — compare against p99 turn duration and the Go runtime row to see if the service is falling behind.
panels.title: Turns in flight

panels.description: Turn completion rate, split by outcome (success/error/timeout/cancelled/client_error). Use this to see WHICH outcome is behind a change in the headline 'Turn rate' or 'Turn error %' — e.g. a spike in timeout points at something slow downstream, while a spike in cancelled usually means clients are disconnecting mid-turn.
panels.title: Turn rate by outcome

panels.description: Turns split by the specific code path that produced their result: 8 explicit named values describing how a turn concluded gracefully (handoff, endCall, transfer, groundingShortCircuit, onSearchFailureDecline, signalRecordOnly, agentTools, directResponse), or — when none of those ran — a fallback that reuses one of outcome's 5 values instead of an empty string (13 possible strings total, not 9). This does NOT distinguish *why* a turn failed: a validation failure, an LLM error, and a mid-loop failure all land in the same fallback bucket as their outcome (e.g. 'error'), giving no more detail than the outcome panel above. Use this to see the shape of graceful turn endings, not to diagnose a failure.
panels.title: Exit-path breakdown

panels.description: Successful-turn latency at three percentiles. p50 is the typical experience; p95/p99 show how bad the tail gets. A rising p50 means turns are uniformly slower (systemic); a rising p99 with a flat p50 means a subset of turns are much slower than the rest — check the heatmap next to this for the shape of that tail.
panels.title: Turn duration: p50/p95/p99

panels.description: The full distribution of successful-turn durations over time, not just percentiles — each column is one time bucket, colored by how many turns landed in each duration range. Use this to see whether slow turns are a single persistent band (e.g. all turns using one particular tool) or a diffuse tail (general slowness), which the p50/p95/p99 line panel can't show on its own.
panels.title: Turn duration heatmap

panels.description: How many times a turn called the LLM, at the median and 95th percentile. Most turns need very few LLM calls; a rising p95 means more turns are looping through multiple LLM round-trips (tool-calling loops, grounding retries) — cross-check 'Loop caps hit' to see if turns are hitting the iteration cap rather than converging naturally.
panels.title: LLM rounds per turn

panels.description: How many tool calls a turn dispatched, at the median and 95th percentile, across all tool kinds. Rising values mean agents are using more tools per conversation — on its own this isn't good or bad, but if it climbs together with 'Tool error %' or p99 turn duration, tool usage is likely what's driving those.
panels.title: Tools per turn

panels.description: How often a turn-internal loop (skill activation, grounding, or agent-tool rounds) hit its iteration cap instead of finishing normally, by loop type. Hitting a cap means the agent gave up looping rather than converging — a rising rate here is a leading indicator that turns are about to start timing out or erroring, ahead of that showing up in the headline error rate.
panels.title: Loop caps hit

panels.description: How many events were in a session's history when it was loaded, at the median and 99th percentile. Session history becomes part of the LLM prompt, so a growing p99 here is an early warning of prompt-token growth and, eventually, of hitting MongoDB's 16MB document size ceiling for very long-running sessions.
panels.title: Session history size at load

panels.description: LLM call rate split by which backend served it (direct, gateway, or sidecar). Use this to see the traffic mix across backends, and to spot a backend's traffic dropping to zero unexpectedly (its calls may be failing before reaching the provider) or a fallback backend suddenly carrying load it doesn't normally serve.
panels.title: LLM request rate by backend

panels.description: LLM failure rate, broken down by the specific reason the backend reported (finish/error reason). This is the drill-down from the headline 'LLM failure %' — a spike concentrated in one reason points at a specific, fixable cause (a rate limit, an auth failure, a context-length error) rather than a generic outage.
panels.title: LLM failure % by reason

panels.description: 95th-percentile LLM call latency, per backend, successful calls only (timeouts are excluded so they don't distort what 'slow but working' looks like). Compare backends against each other here — a consistently slower backend is useful evidence for routing/fallback decisions.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, backend) (rate(cognigy_agents_llm_request_duration_seconds_bucket{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", outcome="success"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: LLM request p95 by backend

panels.description: Token throughput, split into prompt (input) and completion (output) tokens per second. completion already includes reasoning tokens, and cached_prompt is a subset of prompt so it's deliberately left out here to avoid double-counting. A rising prompt rate with flat completion often means growing conversation history (see 'Session history size at load'); a rising completion rate usually means longer model responses.
panels.title: Tokens/s: prompt vs completion

panels.description: How often the LLM gateway's fallback mechanism activated, by reason. Fallback activating occasionally under provider hiccups is normal; a sustained rise means the primary provider/model is degraded often enough that the gateway keeps having to reroute — worth escalating if it stays elevated.
panels.title: LLM fallback events by reason

panels.description: What fraction of LLM calls were served by a fallback provider instead of the primary one — i.e. how often the primary path is actually being used versus routed around. Ratio of two independently-rated counters (cognigy_agents_llm_fallback_active_calls_total / cognigy_agents_llm_requests_total, the latter further split by a dynamic reason label into several child series). Only statistically meaningful under sustained, steady traffic. Under sparse/bursty low-volume traffic (e.g. manual local testing) this can transiently read >100%, even though the raw cumulative counters always satisfy fallback <= successful <= total — not a bug, an expected artifact of rate()-ing near-empty counters.
panels.title: % of calls served under fallback

panels.description: Agent tool-call rate, split by tool kind (builtin_native, builtin_secure, managed, extension, mcp, tool_flow, grounding, skill, or unknown for a tool that never resolved). Use this to see which kinds of tools your agents actually use, and to spot a kind dropping to zero unexpectedly, or 'unknown' climbing — which means tool calls are failing to resolve to a real tool before they even execute.
panels.title: Tool call rate by kind

panels.description: Tool call failure rate, split by kind. In-band errors — a tool that reports failure inside an otherwise-normal response — are folded into this as outcome=error too, so it reflects real failures the caller can't easily see from a raw transport error rate. Use this to find which specific kind of tool is unreliable, rather than only knowing 'something with tools is broken' from the headline.

targets.expr: sum by (kind) (rate(cognigy_agents_tool_calls_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", outcome="error"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (kind) (rate(cognigy_agents_tool_calls_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Tool error % by kind

panels.description: Tool failures split by the specific category of failure (e.g. connection unresolved, extension unresolved, handoff refused, bad arguments, the tool itself reported an error, and several skill-specific categories). This is the drill-down from 'Tool error % by kind' — use it to tell a configuration problem (connection_unresolved) apart from the tool's own logic failing (tool_reported_error).
panels.title: Tool error categories

panels.description: 95th-percentile tool dispatch latency, by kind. A handoff's skipped sibling calls (tools that were never actually dispatched because a handoff intercepted the turn) are excluded, so this only reflects real dispatch time. A builtin tool should be fast; a slow extension or MCP tool points at the remote system it calls out to.
panels.title: Tool call p95 by kind

panels.description: Outcomes of tool executions that ran through the serverless runtime (managed and extension tools), split into success, tool_error (the tool's own code reported failure), transport_error (the serverless call itself failed), timeout, and cancelled. This is the only place you can tell 'the tool's code failed' apart from 'the platform failed to run it' — useful for routing an incident to the right owner.
panels.title: Serverless tool execution outcomes

panels.description: Handoff attempts between the agent and a Cognigy Flow, split by direction (to_flow / from_flow) and outcome (completed or refused outbound; imported or duplicate inbound). Use this to see how often conversations move between agent and flow, and whether outbound handoffs land (completed) or get turned away (refused — see the reasons panel next to this).
panels.title: Handoff outcomes

panels.description: Why an outbound handoff-to-flow was refused, by reason (9 closed reasons — e.g. feature disabled, flow reference missing, the handoff store isn't connected, the hop ceiling was hit, or the payload was too large). A refusal means the conversation stayed with the agent instead of moving to the flow as requested — a persistent single reason usually points at a configuration issue (store_not_connected pairs with the 'Handoff store connected' panel below).
panels.title: Handoff refusal reasons

panels.description: Whether every service-agents pod has a live connection to the Redis store handoffs depend on (1 = connected, 0 = not). Uses the minimum across pods, not an average, specifically so one degraded pod can't be hidden by the rest being healthy. If this drops to 0, expect handoff refusals with reason=store_not_connected / store_read_failed / write_failed to follow — this series doesn't exist at all if this deployment doesn't have handoffs enabled.
panels.title: Handoff store connected

panels.description: Outbound RabbitMQ RPC call rate, by routing key (each key is a different downstream — extensions, connections, LLM model lookups, etc). Runtime-surface calls only, i.e. calls made while executing a turn — this same RPC client's management-surface calls (CRUD audit events, etc.) are broken out on the Management dashboard instead, so the two don't mix on one panel. A routing key dropping to zero when it shouldn't, or climbing unexpectedly, points at a specific downstream worth investigating.
panels.title: RabbitMQ RPC rate by routing key

panels.description: 95th-percentile latency of outbound RabbitMQ RPC calls, by routing key, runtime surface only. A consistently slow routing key means that downstream (service-resources, service-security, etc.) is a candidate for adding to turn latency — compare against the 'p99 turn duration' headline panel.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, routing_key) (rate(cognigy_agents_rpc_request_duration_seconds_bucket{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", surface="runtime"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.title: RabbitMQ RPC p95 by routing key

panels.description: How service-agents' own calls to the service-builtin-resources-go service turn out, by method (ExecuteTool / ListResources) and outcome (success, unavailable, not_found, tool_error, other). 'unavailable' specifically means service-agents couldn't reach that service at all — a sustained run of it is the trigger condition for the BuiltinResourcesUnavailable alert, and means builtin/native tools are effectively unusable until it clears.
panels.title: builtin-resources client outcomes

panels.description: 95th-percentile latency of service-agents' calls to service-builtin-resources-go, by method. Use this to see whether builtin tool executions (routed through this client) are contributing meaningfully to turn latency.
panels.title: builtin-resources client p95 by method

panels.description: The share of MongoDB session-storage calls that failed, by operation (8 operations — read/write/append, etc). not_found is deliberately excluded from 'error' here, since a cache-miss-style 'no session yet' Read during getOrCreateSession is completely normal, not a failure. A real rise here is one of the only aggregate signals that session/event writes are silently failing, since most writes are fire-and-forget — this is how you'd actually notice.

targets.expr: sum by (operation) (rate(cognigy_agents_session_storage_operations_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", outcome="error"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (operation) (rate(cognigy_agents_session_storage_operations_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Session storage error rate by operation

panels.description: 95th-percentile MongoDB session-storage latency, by operation. A slow session store adds directly to turn latency on every turn that loads or saves session state, so a rise here is worth checking against 'p99 turn duration'.
panels.title: Session storage p95 by operation

panels.description: The ExecuteTurn gRPC stream, by result code (e.g. OK, Cancelled, DeadlineExceeded, Internal). This is the transport-level view of the same turns counted in the 'Turns' row above, from the gRPC server's perspective rather than the application's — useful for confirming whether a turn failure was visible at the wire level, versus only in the application's own outcome classification (the two can occasionally disagree in a couple of narrow, documented edge cases outside this metric's own observation point).
panels.title: ExecuteTurn stream rate by code

panels.description: 95th-percentile gRPC-level handling time for the ExecuteTurn stream. This includes time the connection is simply open/streaming, so it isn't a direct substitute for 'p99 turn duration' above — use both together; a persistent gap between them can indicate time spent outside the turn's own timing (e.g. waiting for the stream to open).
panels.title: ExecuteTurn handling p95

panels.description: How often each builtin tool (identified by its slug) was executed, and with what outcome (success, error, not_found, misrouted, internal). A slug you expect traffic for showing nothing at all usually means it isn't being called yet, not that it's broken — check the 'Registered resources' table below to confirm it's even registered.
panels.title: Executions by slug/outcome

panels.description: 95th-percentile execution time, per builtin tool slug. Each builtin tool typically calls out to a different backend (search-orchestrator, email, HTTP, etc.), so use this to find which specific tool is slow rather than treating 'builtin tools' as one thing.
panels.title: Execution p95 by slug

panels.description: A live inventory of every builtin tool, secure tool, and skill this service-builtin-resources-go instance registered successfully at startup — one row per resource. A resource you expect to see that's missing from this table was warn-and-skipped during startup (missing config, an unreachable dependency) — exactly the gap the BuiltinResourceMissing alert is designed to catch.
panels.title: Registered resources

panels.description: service-builtin-resources-go's own gRPC server, by result code. Unavailable codes during pod startup are expected — the readiness interceptor deliberately rejects calls before the service is ready — so don't read a burst of Unavailable at deploy time as a real problem; sustained Unavailable outside a rollout is worth investigating.
panels.title: gRPC codes

panels.description: Outbound RabbitMQ RPC call rate from service-builtin-resources-go to service-resources/service-security, by routing key. Same shared decorator as the service-agents RPC panels above, just under this service's own metric namespace — use it the same way, to spot a specific downstream dependency degrading.
panels.title: RPC to service-resources/security: rate

panels.description: 95th-percentile latency of those same outbound RPC calls. A slow dependency here adds directly to the execution time of whichever builtin tool needed that lookup.
panels.title: RPC to service-resources/security: p95

panels.description: Setting values each pod rejected from its reloadable config file in the last 10 minutes because they do not parse (cognigy_reloadable_config_callback_errors_total{kind="parse"}). Running pods keep the previous value; a pod that starts while the value is in the file stops at start-up. Any value above 0 is what the AgentsV2ConfigValueRejected alert fires on.
panels.title: Rejected setting values

panels.description: When each pod last read a change to its reloadable config file (cognigy_reloadable_config_last_change_timestamp_seconds). It moves on any change to the file, including other services' platform keys and a value the pod then rejected, so it shows that the pod has read the file, not that every value in it is in use. After a config change, a pod whose time is older has not read the file yet. 'none since start' means the pod has read no change since it started.
panels.title: Last config file change, per pod

panels.description: The restart coordinator, which rolls a Deployment when a setting read only at start-up changes in the file (today only builtin-resources declares such settings). 'pending' is 1 on a builtin-resources pod while a restart is held back (manual policy, or waiting for its window); the other lines count restart events in the last 10 minutes. 'forbidden' means the pod was refused permission to patch its own Deployment.
panels.title: Restart coordinator

panels.description: Turn rate broken down by organisation and project, filtered by the Organisation/Project variables above. Use this to see which tenants are actually driving traffic, or to isolate a single customer's behavior when investigating a tenant-specific report.
panels.title: Turns by project

panels.description: How often a brand-new session was created, by organisation and project — this is the platform's actual 'conversation' count, distinct from 'Turns by project' which counts every message exchange within those conversations.
panels.title: New conversations by project

panels.description: Average turns per new conversation, computed as turn rate divided by new-conversation rate, per organisation/project. A rising value means conversations are getting longer (more back-and-forth per session); a value that swings wildly usually just means conversation volume for that tenant is too low right now for the ratio to be stable — read it as a trend over a wider time range rather than an instantaneous number.

targets.expr: sum by (organisationId, projectId) (rate(cognigy_agents_turns_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", organisationId=~"$organisationId", projectId=~"$projectId"}[$__rate_interval])) / clamp_min(sum by (organisationId, projectId) (rate(cognigy_agents_sessions_started_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", organisationId=~"$organisationId", projectId=~"$projectId"}[$__rate_interval])), 0.001)

panels.title: Turns per conversation

panels.description: LLM token throughput (prompt + completion; completion already includes reasoning, and cached_prompt is excluded as a subset of prompt) by organisation and project. This is the closest proxy this dashboard has to LLM cost/usage per tenant.

targets.expr: sum by (organisationId, projectId) (rate(cognigy_agents_llm_tokens_total{cluster="$cluster", namespace="$namespace", organisationId=~"$organisationId", projectId=~"$projectId", kind=~"prompt|completion"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Tokens by project

panels.description: Tool call rate by organisation and project. Use this alongside 'Tokens by project' and 'Turns by project' to build a full usage profile for a specific tenant.
panels.title: Tool calls by project

panels.description: Number of live goroutines per pod, over time. Go handles thousands of goroutines fine on its own, so an isolated number doesn't matter much — what matters is the trend: a steady, unbounded climb (rather than settling to a stable baseline) usually means something is leaking goroutines (a context or channel that's never cleaned up), not normal request-driven fluctuation.
panels.title: Goroutines

panels.description: Memory the Go runtime's heap is actively using, per pod. Look for the same pattern as goroutines: healthy is fluctuating-but-bounded (rising under load, falling back after garbage collection); a heap that only ever grows and never comes back down after GC is the signature of a memory leak — worth catching before it turns into an OOM (see 'RSS vs limit' for the container-level view of that same risk).
panels.title: Go heap in-use

panels.description: Go garbage-collector pause durations, at several quantiles (each line is one quantile, labelled by the 'quantile' value). GC pauses briefly stop the world, so a rising pause duration adds directly to tail latency on whatever request happens to be running at that moment — worth checking against 'p99 turn duration' if that's also drifting up.
panels.title: GC pause quantiles

panels.description: Actual container memory usage (working set) against the Kubernetes memory limit, per pod. The important thing is the gap: usage climbing toward the limit line means the pod is heading toward an OOM kill, at which point it restarts and drops whatever turns were in flight.
panels.title: RSS vs limit

panels.description: Actual CPU usage against the Kubernetes CPU request and limit, per pod. Usage consistently near or above the limit line means the pod is being CPU-throttled — a common, easy-to-miss cause of turns getting slower with no change in error rate, since throttling delays requests rather than failing them.
panels.title: CPU vs request/limit

panels.description: Open file descriptors against this pod's file descriptor limit. Climbing steadily toward the limit — rather than staying flat under normal load — is the signature of an fd leak (connections or files opened but never closed); hitting the limit causes the process to start failing to open new connections/files entirely.
panels.title: Open file descriptors
